decision_log.question: How should acceptance tests be distributed across milestones?
decision_log.choice: Phase 1 gates on input-contract and audit-spine tests (AT1-AT3, AT4 subset, AT5, AT8, AT9, AT19, AT20); Phase 2 gates on patchset/role-separation tests (AT12-AT14, AT22); Phase 3 gates on integration/repair/change-control tests (AT10, AT15, AT16); Phase 4 gates on remaining tests and full suite
decision_log.rationale: Each phase gates on the acceptance tests most relevant to its deliverables. Phase 1 validates the foundation (input contracts, audit spine, secrets, tool permissions). Phase 2 validates parallel execution mechanics (patchsets, role separation). Phase 3 validates integration-specific concerns (evidence pointers across integration, smallest-passing-repair, change control). Phase 4 validates end-to-end closure including judge, freeze, workspace integrity, and flaky-failure handling.
alternatives_considered: Run full AT suite at every phase — excessive for early phases that lack later components
Defer all AT validation to Phase 4 — loses early feedback on foundation correctness
what_would_change_this_decision: Acceptance test dependencies change such that earlier tests require later components
Regulatory requirements mandate full suite validation at each phase boundary

decision_log.question: How should K12 (merge conflicts from parallel lanes) be mitigated?
decision_log.choice: Deterministic merge ordering algorithm in C18 (Phase 3) that produces identical results regardless of lane completion order, with strict conflict escalation thresholds triggering reroute/HITL
decision_log.rationale: K12 is the primary elevated risk for O2. The deterministic merge ordering algorithm ensures reproducibility by making integration results independent of wall-clock timing. Strict escalation thresholds prevent automated conflict resolution from producing unsafe merges. This directly resolves alignment warning AL006.
alternatives_considered: Optimistic merge with manual conflict resolution only — not deterministic, violates reproducibility requirements
Lane priority ordering based on dependency graph — insufficient when lanes have overlapping file sets
Rebase-based integration — more complex and still requires deterministic ordering rules
what_would_change_this_decision: Conflict rates are consistently zero in practice, making the algorithm unnecessary
A proven deterministic rebase strategy becomes available that handles all edge cases
Target repos have strict module boundaries that eliminate overlap entirely

decision_log.rationale: Parallel execution introduces additional complexity vectors (lane isolation, merge conflicts, distributed role separation) that warrant high human oversight. decision_log.question: How should workspace partitioning work for parallel lanes?
decision_log.choice: Per-lane namespaced workspace partitions managed by C22 with a shared canonical integration partition used only during the integration sub-flow
decision_log.rationale: Per-lane partitions enforce isolation during parallel execution, preventing cross-lane contamination (K8 mitigation). The shared integration partition is activated only when C18 begins deterministic merge, ensuring a single governed merge point. workspace_index.json spans all partitions with provenance metadata for full auditability.

supplemental_evaluations.title: Risk Posture Assessment for O2 Parallel Architecture
supplemental_evaluations.notes: K12 (merge conflicts) is the primary elevated risk for O2 and is directly addressed in Phase 3 with the deterministic merge ordering algorithm. K8 (workspace integrity) risk is higher due to namespaced partitions but mitigated by C22 partition enforcement and workspace integrity validators in Phase 1. K10 (role separation) risk increases with parallel pods but is mitigated by per-lane orchestrator-enforced output-type allowlists validated in Phase 2. K9 (context pack overflow) risk is actually lower per-lane due to smaller scoped packs. K6 (flaky tests) risk is distributed across lanes but integration revalidation in Phase 3 can amplify it; deterministic retry budgets and quarantine policies apply. Overall risk profile is manageable with the hybrid phased approach, but depends on resolution of blocking open questions Q7-Q9.

glossary.definition: A CouncilOS subsystem that consumes a frozen planning output (plan_package_final.json) and produces audited, reproducible repository changes and release artifacts under orchestrator-controlled policies and validators.

The canonical, typed/versioned set of JSON artifacts emitted at freeze, including run manifest, event log, work plan, patchsets, repo snapshot, test/quality/trace/review/release artifacts, decision record, and required workspace artifacts (workspace_index, context_packs, stage_handoffs).

A tool-accessible, versioned and auditable storage area treated as an extension of the artifact system, containing canonical JSON artifacts and explicitly non-canonical notes/summaries, governed by permissions, retention, and checkpoint/resume handoffs.

An RFC 6901 JSON Pointer object {artifact_ref, entity_id|null, json_pointer, note} referencing a versioned JSON artifact location; used as the sole standard for traceability across decisions, findings, and state representations.

A required JSON artifact emitted at each checkpoint boundary capturing resumable state: objectives, completed work, pending blockers, next actions, and pointers into canonical artifacts (work plan, patchsets, validation outputs).

A canonical artifact proposed when plan semantics would need to change; requires explicit decisioning and policy-triggered escalation (HITL and/or reroute upstream) before any semantic deviation is allowed.
Deterministic code component with sole authority over routing, budgets, iteration limits, termination, checkpoint/resume, tool permissions, selection logic, and validator enforcement.
A bounded, deterministically-compiled set of workspace artifacts provided to a role at a stage, selected by explicit rules and cited via evidence pointers.
A JSON artifact embedding code diffs with deterministic apply order for repo modifications; used as the sole mechanism for code repair/changes in the workflow.
A code-owned deterministic gate that checks artifact integrity/completeness and quality criteria to allow stage transitions or freeze.
